title: Neck & Forearms - Charles Smith (1951)
author: Mithosphere
desc:
I remember a discussion a friend of mine and I had some months ago. “The pictures you have of those muscle boys in your magazines are all, more or less, stripped down to bathing trunks. There’s no difficulty in seeing what they are - lifters. But, what about a fellow walking along the street? Is there any way in which you can tell he is above average in strength and development?" 

There’s one way I can ALWAYS tell if a man is in good physical shape, above average in power and muscular development or, a strength athlete - his NECK. And when you come to close quarters, there’s another way - his GRIP. Look at the neck of a boxer or wrestler, particularly the latter, it’s full, thick and powerful in appearance. Now take a glance at the neck of a guy who has been sick for a long time, or the neck of an old man: scrawny, stringy, muscular tone very poor. Beyond any doubt, the condition of a man’s neck indicates his condition of vitality and virility.

Then there’s a man’s grip. It is a decided social advantage to have a grip that appears sincere and firm. And so we see that the neck is the visible manifestation of a man’s condition and the grip the hidden one, not only of things physical but mental and emotional.

Neck work, and forearms too, are just about the most satisfying exercises you can perform. Strangely, these sections of the physique are looked on as “difficult” parts and are ranked with the calves as being hard to develop. Actually, it takes no longer than four to six weeks of specialization to produce an appreciable increase in neck and forearm size.

There are many ways of increasing the size of the neck and forearms. In my opinion the very best of all neck movements are performed on an exercise bench. The same goes for forearms, with but one exception - heavy deadlifts on a thick bar. The head strap has its uses too but the resistance applied to the neck by a training partner, CONTROLLED resistance, is perhaps the best means of developing to the full the muscles of the neck.

Both sections of the physique can stand an extremely large amount of work, so don’t be afraid to exercise them often and with great vigor. You will find the neck gets much stiffer than the forearms, obviously because it isn’t used as much as the hands and lower arms are, so as soon as you feel the muscles tightening up, quit neck work and get going on the forearms returning when the tightness wears off. During the day, especially the day AFTER the workout, tensing, turning and twisting the neck muscles and head will help take the stiffness away and keep the muscles “warmed up” for the next workout.

The best time for you to use these exercises is right after you have completed your usual barbell workout. Take it easy the first few workouts so you don’t suffer too much discomfort from sore neck muscles. When your neck and forearm muscles are broken into the idea of working really hard, you can start to go to town and build up a neck of which you can be proud.

ex.note: Slow and deliberate. Lie face-down on bench. Lower head, then turn to right and raise and lower. Do the same on the left. Add weight when you can do 3x20.
Lie on bench facing up. Don't allow shoulders and upper back to leave bench. Lower head and then raise until the chin touches the chest.
Pull head from one shoulder to another - best used on a cable setup. AMRAP per side. If you feel capable of doing more set, do up to 6.
Single End Dumbbell: Grip as far to end as possible. Rest elbow on bench, forearm pointing up. Rotate wrist in a complete circle. AMRAPs per side. As many sets as you want.
Rest forearm on bench, slight decline, palm up. Don't let dumbbell roll out of hand.
Close grip, rest forearms on bench, palms down. Thumbs around bar.
